segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Be careful not to practice your righteousness in front of people in order to be seen by them; otherwise you have no reward with your Father who is in the heavens.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: So when you give to the needy, do not sound a trumpet ahead of you, as the performers do in the synagogues and in the streets, so that they may be praised by people. Truly I tell you, they have been paid their reward in full.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But when you give to the needy, do not let your left hand know what your right hand is doing,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: so that your giving may be in secret; and your Father who sees in secret will repay you.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And when you pray, you are not to be like the performers; for they love to pray standing in the synagogues and on the corners of the main streets, so that they may be seen by people. Truly I tell you, they have been paid their reward in full.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But you, when you pray, go into your inner room, shut your door, and pray to your Father who is in secret; and your Father who sees in secret will repay you.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And when you pray, do not babble on like the Gentiles, for they think that they will be heard because of their many words.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: So do not be like them, for your Father knows what you need before you ask him.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: So you are to pray like this: ‘Our Father in the heavens, may your name be held holy,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: may your kingdom come, may your will be done, as in heaven, so also on earth.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Give us today our daily bread,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: and forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors;

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: and do not bring us into testing, but rescue us from the evil one.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: For if you forgive people their offenses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you;

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: but if you do not forgive people, neither will your Father forgive your offenses.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And when you fast, do not put on a gloomy face like the performers, for they make their faces unsightly so that they may be seen by people to be fasting. Truly I tell you, they have been paid their reward in full.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But you, when you fast, put oil on your head and wash your face,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: so that you may not be seen by people to be fasting, but by your Father who is in secret; and your Father who sees in secret will repay you.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Do not store up treasures for yourselves on earth, where moth and rust destroy, and where thieves break in and steal;

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: but store up treasures for yourselves in heaven, where neither moth nor rust destroys, and where thieves do not break in or steal;

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: for where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: The lamp of the body is the eye. So if your eye is generous, your whole body will be full of light;

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: but if your eye is stingy, your whole body will be full of darkness. So if the light in you is darkness, how great is that darkness!

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: No one can serve as a slave to two masters; for either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will be devoted to the one and despise the other. You cannot serve as slaves to both God and Mammon.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: For this reason I tell you: do not worry about your life, what you will eat, or about your body, what you will wear. Is not life more than food, and the body more than clothing?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Look at the birds of the sky: they do not sow or reap or gather into barns, and yet your heavenly Father feeds them. Are you not worth much more than they are?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And which of you by worrying can add a single cubit to the length of your life?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And why do you worry about clothing? Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow: they do not toil or spin.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Yet I tell you that not even Solomon in all his glory was clothed like one of these.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But if God so clothes the grass of the field, which is here today and tomorrow is thrown into the oven, will he not much more clothe you, you of little faith?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: So do not worry, saying, ‘What are we to eat?’ or ‘What are we to drink?’ or ‘What are we to wear?’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: For the Gentiles seek after all these things, and your heavenly Father knows that you need them all.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But seek first his kingdom and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: So do not worry about tomorrow, for tomorrow will worry about itself. Each day has enough trouble of its own.

notes.traditional: righteousness (KJV: alms, following a different Greek text)
notes.note: Here the word means the practice of religious duty, and the verse is a heading for the three examples that follow: giving to the needy, prayer and fasting. Greek has a single word-family where English divides between righteous/just and righteousness/justice. Later manuscripts read “almsgiving” in place of “righteousness” here, which is why the King James Version has “alms”.
The Greek is plural, a Semitic turn of phrase that Matthew uses regularly for God's dwelling. Most translations flatten it to “heaven”. This translation keeps the plural where the Greek has it.

The Greek word originally meant a stage actor, though in Jewish Greek before the New Testament it had already come to mean a godless or insincere person, and most translations render “hypocrites” throughout. In this chapter the picture of an audience is in the context itself (trumpets, street corners, being seen), so “performers” is used here and in verses 5 and 16. Elsewhere this translation keeps “hypocrites”.

notes.phrase: they have been paid their reward in full
notes.note: The verb is the standard term on surviving receipts from the period for acknowledging payment in full, so hearers would have caught a commercial tone: the account is settled and nothing more is owed. Many modern translations render it similarly, “they have received their reward in full”. The same picture lies behind the Father who “will repay” in verses 4, 6 and 18, traditionally “will reward”.

notes.traditional: use vain repetitions (KJV); heap up empty phrases
notes.note: The Greek verb is extremely rare and its exact meaning is uncertain. It may imitate the sound of stammering or meaningless chatter. The next clause, “because of their many words”, shows that the fault in view is piling up words to gain a hearing; whether repetition as such is meant is not clear.

notes.phrase: may your name be held holy
notes.note: “Hallowed” is now archaic and can be heard as a statement rather than a request. The Greek is a petition that God's name be treated as holy. Many scholars take the passive as asking God himself to act to vindicate his name, as in Ezekiel 36:23. The three opening petitions share the same grammatical form, which “may ...” reproduces.

The meaning of this Greek word is unknown. It is almost unattested outside the Lord's Prayer, and ancient Christian writers were already unsure of it. The main proposals are “for the coming day”, “necessary for existence” and “for today”. With no secure alternative, the traditional “daily” is kept.

The Greek word covers both a trial that tests a person's faithfulness and an enticement to do wrong; in the period, and in the Septuagint, the first sense is the usual one. “Temptation” suggests to a modern reader only the second, and raises the puzzle of God tempting people. Many scholars and some recent translations prefer “testing” or “the time of trial”, though “temptation” remains the most familiar rendering.

The Greek form can be masculine (“the evil one”, that is, the devil) or neuter (“evil” in general), and grammar cannot decide between them. Matthew elsewhere uses the phrase for the devil (13:19, 38), and most recent translations take it that way here, but “deliver us from evil” is equally possible.

notes.phrase: rescue us from the evil one
notes.traditional: For thine is the kingdom, and the power, and the glory, for ever. Amen.
notes.note: The familiar closing doxology is absent from the earliest manuscripts of Matthew and from the oldest commentaries on the prayer. It appears in varying forms in later manuscripts and is generally thought to have been added from the prayer's use in worship. The Greek text translated here ends the prayer at this point.

The word means “single, sincere”, and its word-family is used for open-handed giving. The “evil eye” of the next verse is a known Jewish idiom for stinginess, rendered there as “stingy” because the English phrase “evil eye” now suggests a curse. Most translations keep the physical image with “healthy” and “unhealthy” and mention generosity in a footnote. The saying sits between treasure in heaven and serving Mammon, which favours the reading about money, but the physical image of the eye is lost in this rendering.

The verb means to be someone's slave, not merely to work for them. The point of the saying depends on it: a hired worker can have two employers, but a slave is owned by one master. Several modern translations now use “slave” language; others keep “serve” to avoid association with race-based chattel slavery.

Mammon is an Aramaic word for wealth or property, which Matthew's Greek leaves untranslated. Here it is pictured as a rival master who owns slaves, which is why the word is kept as a name. It does not in itself mean ill-gotten wealth, and there is no good evidence that it was the name of a deity.

notes.phrase: add a single cubit to the length of your life
notes.traditional: add one cubit unto his stature (KJV); add a single hour to his span of life
notes.note: The Greek noun can mean either age or bodily height, and a cubit is a measure of length, about half a metre. “Add a cubit to his height” is therefore possible, but a cubit of height would be a huge addition, not the trifle the argument requires. Most modern translations take it as a measure of length applied figuratively to a lifetime, as here.

notes.traditional: the kingdom of God, and his righteousness
notes.note: Most manuscripts read “the kingdom of God and his righteousness”. The Greek text translated here follows early witnesses that lack “of God”, so that “his” refers back to the heavenly Father of the previous verse. The sense is the same either way.

candidates.reason: Jesus' formula “Amen I say to you” recurs throughout the Gospels and translators vary between truly, I assure you, amen and solemnly, so one rendering is needed.
The word ordinarily means wages or pay, and the choice between “reward” and “wages” affects many sayings in the Gospels, Paul and Revelation, especially alongside the receipt term ἀπέχω.
The noun and its verb πειράζω shift between “test/trial” and “tempt/temptation” in English translations across the Gospels, James, Hebrews and 1 Peter, and readers are misled when the English varies.
The plural (with the related ἐθνικός in verse 7) can be rendered Gentiles, nations or pagans, and the choice needs to be consistent across the Gospels, Acts and Paul.
The word is rendered “life”, “soul” or “self” in different passages, and the traditional “soul” often imports a body–soul dualism the Greek does not imply.

warnings: Verse 2: ἀπέχω is not rendered with a register form (have been paid in full; be far from / abstain from) and has no register-exception note.
Verse 5: ἀπέχω is not rendered with a register form (have been paid in full; be far from / abstain from) and has no register-exception note.
Verse 16: ἀπέχω is not rendered with a register form (have been paid in full; be far from / abstain from) and has no register-exception note.
